{"markdown":"# What changed: research loops became more inspectable

*Research Loop — As of 2026-10-14*

For students considering research agents, the useful development in these reports is a clearer way to delegate bounded experiments: define what may change, preserve what happened, and compare the result under controlled conditions. Our interpretation is that these practices justify testing automated searches while keeping the research objective and scientific interpretation in human hands. They do not establish that greater autonomy produces more discovery per unit of compute. <!-- 01-c6 -->

The supplied publication metadata places these reports within the run’s 30-day UTC window ending October 13, 2026. That dates the reports, not necessarily their experiments. Agora’s account appeared in September, but its campaign ran from April 26 to May 8. Its recent contribution is therefore the documented account of that earlier work. [Agora](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094). <!-- 01-c1 -->

Agora makes the experimental record its organizing principle. The authors describe Git commits that preserve results, hypotheses, insights, verifications and reports, with links to the prior contributions they build upon. For a student, our reading is that this offers a useful standard for inspectability: a reported result should lead back to its artifacts and ancestry. A score alone cannot provide that history. [Agora, abstract and contribution graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094). <!-- 01-c1 --> <!-- 01-c6 -->

AutoMIP adds a complementary requirement: a promising hypothesis needs a compatible execution state. Its proposed search layer chooses whether to refine a direction or switch, identifies an appropriate historical starting point, restores its artifacts and registers the experiment before execution. [AutoMIP, §3.3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39360). <!-- 01-c2 --> Read together, the systems suggest distinguishing the history that explains a result from the saved state needed to continue experimenting. For a small project, we would preserve both the rationale for a change and the exact version from which it ran. <!-- 01-c6 -->

The solar-panel segmentation study provides a concrete boundary for delegation. It applies an existing protocol in which the agent edits only the training program, keeps a change when the validation metric improves and otherwise reverts. Its three campaigns were each capped at 24 logged experiments, including the baseline. The one-hour training allowance applies to each trial, not the entire campaign. [Segmentation study, §§1–3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491). <!-- 01-c5 -->

Those boundaries also determine what the experiment can establish. With the architecture and evaluator frozen, the authors characterize the loop as close to code-level hyperparameter search, although proposals can extend beyond a predefined parameter space. For students, this is a useful task to automate: searching training changes against a declared evaluator. It leaves open whether the evaluator captures the scientific question worth answering. [Segmentation study, §2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491). <!-- 01-c6 -->

NanoProteinLM makes the human decision point explicit. Its authors report that sequential recipe search increased long-range contact precision from 28.2% to 36.6% P@L at the same 48.4B-token training budget, with a human choosing which recipes to scale. This supports a bounded claim about a training recipe; it does not demonstrate fully autonomous biological discovery. [NanoProteinLM, “A better PLM recipe by hill-climbing”](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/). <!-- 01-c3 --> Equal final training-token budgets also do not establish equal total search costs. Our practical interpretation is to distinguish the resources spent finding a recipe from those spent validating the selected recipe. <!-- 01-c3 --> <!-- 01-c6 -->

Malena supplies a reason to test a simple agent before investing in elaborate orchestration. Its comparison holds compute resources, time budgets and backbone models fixed. In its coding-interface experiment, hidden test scores are withheld from agents. These controls make the comparison more informative about the added machinery under the tested conditions. [Malena study, §§4.1 and 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40303). <!-- 01-c4 --> The authors report that a single long-running session was a strong baseline and that their added standard components did not improve on it. That finding supports benchmarking complexity, rather than assuming its value transfers to every research task. [Malena study, conclusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40303). <!-- 01-c6 -->

The cross-source lesson is an experimental contract: specify the permitted edits, evaluator, resource limits, stopping rule and evidence to retain. Our recommendation is to start with a simple baseline, preserve unsuccessful attempts alongside improvements, and require a reviewable comparison before expanding the search. Agora itself says that establishing discovery efficiency requires a matched comparison. Its contribution record demonstrates a way to inspect collaboration; that record alone cannot establish the collaboration’s efficiency. [Agora, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094). <!-- 01-c6 -->

These are separate research accounts, not independent replications of a shared result. The supplied evidence includes neither independent replication nor outside researcher assessment of these findings. Performance figures should therefore remain author-reported results, and the advice here remains an inference: delegate bounded execution and search, while retaining responsibility for what counts as progress and whether the evidence supports that judgment. <!-- 01-c6 -->

## References

- [Agora: Git as Shared Memory for Collective AutoResearch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094). <!-- 01-c1; 01-c6. Editorial disposition: accept for piece 01; concrete contribution ancestry and an explicit efficiency limitation. -->
- [Autoresearch in Mixed-Integer Linear and Nonlinear Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39360). <!-- 01-c2. Editorial disposition: accept for piece 01; specifies hypothesis selection coupled to recoverable execution states. -->
- [Hill-Climbing a Protein Language Model: A Taste of Autoresearch for Scientific Discovery](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/). <!-- 01-c3. Editorial disposition: accept for piece 01; bounded recipe comparison with an explicit human scaling gate. -->
- [How Much of a Harness Does a Strong Agent Need for Autonomous ML Engineering?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40303). <!-- 01-c4; 01-c6. Editorial disposition: accept for piece 01; matched comparisons and a simple-agent baseline. -->
- [Insights from Autoresearch for Solar Panel Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10491). <!-- 01-c5; 01-c6. Editorial disposition: accept for piece 01; constrained edits, explicit trial budgets and a narrow interpretation of search. -->
